name: Affinity bias
statement: People favour those who resemble them in background, interests or demography, and hiring and promotion decisions carry that preference.
meaning: Affinity bias is a term of corporate diversity training rather than of research psychology. A Crossref title search for the phrase on 21 September 2026 returned ten records, and they run from behavioural finance and team-growth modelling to human-robot interaction, large language models and ChIP-seq binding affinity. PubMed returned ten records the same day, none of them a study of a construct by that name. What the term points at is covered by two older literatures that do have evidence behind them. The first is similarity-attraction, which Donn Byrne began measuring in 1961, and which holds that liking rises with similarity of attitudes. The second is in-group favouritism, entry no. 103, which holds that people extend help and resources to members of their own category. Affinity bias adds a third claim on top: that the preference operates inside workplace evaluation, unnoticed by the evaluator. That third claim is where the field evidence thins out.

origin.where: The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
origin.note: No publication coining the name was located. Byrne's paper established the effect the name is applied to. The earliest indexed scholarly use of the exact phrase found in these searches is a 2012 chapter in a behavioural finance textbook, which the publisher's site would not serve, so what the chapter means by the phrase is not stated here.

evidence:
Byrne's 1961 experiment is the root, and it was read for this entry from a scan of the journal volume. Sixty-four students at the University of Texas answered 26 attitude questions, then marked the 13 issues they thought most important. Two weeks later each was handed a stranger's scale, said to come from another class and in fact filled in by the experimenter. The four conditions were not one similarity gradient. One group saw its own answers exactly reproduced, one saw the exact opposite, and the other two crossed agreement with the importance of the issue. Against the group shown opposite answers, the group shown identical answers liked the stranger more, and rated it higher on intelligence, knowledge of current events, morality and adjustment. All six differences passed p < .001, on 17 subjects per group. Byrne printed t tests and no effect size. The Cohen's d of 3.40 usually quoted for this study is Greenwald and Pettigrew's figure, averaged across those six measures. Byrne's third hypothesis, that agreement on important issues counts for more, held on three measures of six.

Rand and Wexley moved the design into hiring in 1975. They video-taped a Black and a White applicant supplying biographical information that either matched a White interviewer's or did not. The 160 raters were not a general sample: they were picked for extreme scores on need for affiliation and on racial prejudice. Biographical similarity raised ratings of job suitability. Neither applicant race nor the rater's need for affiliation produced a main effect, and prejudiced raters marked everybody down.

The strongest positive field result comes from personnel records rather than experiments. Giuliano, Levine and Leonard used the daily records of a large American retailer covering more than 700 stores, more than 1,500 store managers and more than 100,000 entry-level hires between February 1996 and July 1998. Manager turnover let them hold the store fixed. Under non-Black managers the probability that a new hire was Black fell by 3.5 to 4.0 percentage points, which in a typical store moves the Black share of hires from about 21 to 17 percent and the White share from 60 to 64 percent. In a typical southern store the same swap moved the Black share from 29 to 21 percent. Where Hispanics were at least 30 percent of the local population, replacing a Hispanic manager with a White one moved the Hispanic share of hires from about 59 to 48 percent. Below that threshold the two groups of managers hired almost identically.

Rivera's study of elite professional service firms rests on 120 interviews with employers, 40 in each of three industries, and on nine months inside one firm's recruiting department in 2006 and 2007. She was not allowed to sit in on interviews, and observed the deliberations instead. Employers sought candidates who were culturally similar to themselves in leisure pursuits, experiences and self-presentation, and she reports those concerns often outweighing concerns about absolute productivity. The resemblance doing the work there is cultural rather than demographic.

replication.headline: Actual similarity tracks attraction at r = .47 across laboratory and field studies pooled, and two studies of structured job interviews covering 12,203 and 19,931 applicants find no interviewer-applicant similarity effect at all.
replication.detail:
Montoya, Horton and Kirchner meta-analysed 460 effect sizes from 313 laboratory and field investigations. Actual similarity correlated with attraction at r = .47 and perceived similarity at r = .39, both figures pooling the two settings. The breakdown by stage is the useful part. Actual similarity predicted attraction in no-interaction and short-interaction studies, fell once any interaction had occurred, and was not significant in existing relationships. Perceived similarity predicted attraction at every stage. An earlier manuscript by the same three authors, hosted on Horton's university page under the filename of the published article but carrying a different title and a smaller dataset of 385 effect sizes from 293 investigations, cuts the literature by setting instead. It reports r = .536 overall, r = .506 in laboratory studies, 95% CI [.425, .586], and r = .150 in field studies. Applying a publication-bias weight function to the field studies moved the mean from 0.152 to 0.029, an attenuation the authors put at about 81 percent, and left the field effect non-significant, z = 1.37, p = .17. The laboratory funnel plot showed no comparable asymmetry.

The workplace tests run against the term. Sacco, Scheu, Ryan and Schmitt analysed one-on-one highly structured college recruiting interviews with 708 interviewers and 12,203 applicants across seven job families. Hierarchical linear models gave no evidence of race or sex similarity effects, while D-scores and analysis of variance at the individual level did give them, which is a finding about levels of analysis before it is a finding about bias. McCarthy, Van Iddekinge and Campion put the same question to 19,931 applicants and 207 interviewers at an agency of the United States government, where panels of two interviewers were assigned to applicants at random. Their abstract calls the post managerial-level and their method section calls the applicants entry-level candidates for professional positions. Neither applicant demographics nor applicant-interviewer similarity moved interview ratings, effect sizes sat consistently below .10, and pseudo R-squared values were zero. The one significant main effect was small: women scored above men by d = .03 to .04. Both sets of authors attribute the null to interview structure, which leaves little to the interviewer's discretion. Greenwald and Pettigrew cite both studies for the same point.

study.cite: Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., & Kirchner, J. (2008). Is actual similarity necessary for attraction? A meta-analysis of actual and perceived similarity. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 25(6), 889-922.

replicated.weighting: actual similarity, 460 effect sizes from 313 investigations

limits:
The name has no located research base, and that is the first limit. Searches on 21 September 2026 covered Crossref title and bibliographic queries, PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall and web search. An earlier note that OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar answered only with rate-limit errors did not hold: both answered on retry. Wikipedia's article on affinity bias names no coiner and gives no citation for the term's history. Where the phrase does appear in indexed scholarship it usually means something unrelated, from ligand binding to sequencing artefacts.

The published Montoya meta-analysis was still not obtained, and the reason is not the one given before. SAGE answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall notice, an archived capture of the same PDF resolves to a login page, and OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar all record the article as closed. The figures attributed to it here come from the abstract carried by Crossref, which reports no confidence intervals. The earlier manuscript version was read in full, and whether its publication-bias analysis survived into the published article could not be checked, so the two are kept apart above. Sacco and colleagues' article was not obtained either: PsycNet, ResearchGate and CORE all refused, and the account here comes from the abstract at PubMed. Giuliano and colleagues' figures come from the September 2006 working paper hosted at Berkeley, whose abstract matches the published one; the published article at Chicago sits behind a Cloudflare challenge, and two eScholarship records answered with an empty 202. The authors state they cannot disclose exact sample sizes because the employer is anonymous. The Pompian chapter was not read, because Wiley answers with a bot challenge, so no account of what it means by the phrase is given above.
misreadings:
The hiring audit studies are the evidence usually produced, and they do not measure affinity. Bertrand and Mullainathan sent fictitious CVs carrying White-sounding and African-American-sounding names to newspaper advertisements in Boston and Chicago, and White names drew 50 percent more callbacks. Quillian, Pager, Hexel and Midtboen pooled every available field experiment of hiring discrimination against African Americans or Latinos, 28 studies representing 55,842 applications for 26,326 positions. Their headline estimates do not come from that whole pool. They come from the 24 studies with fieldwork since 1989, which cover 54,318 applications for 25,517 positions. On those, Whites drew 36 percent more callbacks than African Americans, 95% CI 25 to 47 percent. They drew 24 percent more than Latinos, 95% CI 15 to 33 percent. Discrimination against African Americans has not fallen since 1989, while the authors find modest evidence of a decline against Latinos. None of that shows recruiters favouring their own. Greenwald and Pettigrew, who argue the favouritism case, enter the same caveat in a footnote. Audit studies do not report their results by the race of the housing agent or hiring manager. Almost all of those agents and managers were surely White, and whether favouritism varied with their own group is unknown.

Giuliano, Levine and Leonard did have the manager's race, and their own reading is not the convenient one. They tested four explanations for their result and could rule none out cleanly. They found no evidence that segregated recruiting networks or efficiency drove it, while noting their tests had low power against those explanations. Their strongest positive finding on mechanism was that many White job-seekers appear to avoid working for non-White managers. An own-group hiring pattern can be produced by who applies as well as by who the manager likes.

A third reading treats affinity bias as a mechanism distinct from in-group favouritism. Greenwald and Pettigrew treat similarity-attraction and the minimal group paradigm as two lines of evidence for a single thesis, that favouritism rather than hostility drives most contemporary discrimination.

A fourth treats demographic resemblance as the strongest form of the effect. Rivera argues the opposite in her own paper. Most of her interview pairs were White evaluating White and male evaluating male, cultural matching operated inside those pairs, and at the firm she observed, women and minorities were hired at higher rates than White and male applicants. Giuliano's Hispanic manager effect appeared only where Hispanics made up at least 30 percent of the local population and vanished below it, so in the one dataset here that could test the demographic version, it was conditional on context.

sources.text: Byrne, D. (1961). Interpersonal attraction and attitude similarity. The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 62(3), 713-715. Read in full from the Internet Archive scan of the bound 1961 volume; the design, the four conditions and the t tests above come from that text.

Greenwald, A. G., & Pettigrew, T. F. (2014). With malice toward none and charity for some: Ingroup favoritism enables discrimination. American Psychologist, 69(7), 669-684. Full text read from the author's hosted copy; the phrase 'affinity bias' does not appear in it, and the Cohen's d of 3.40 for Byrne's study is their calculation, not Byrne's.

Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., & Kirchner, J. (2008). Is actual similarity necessary for attraction? A meta-analysis of actual and perceived similarity. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 25(6), 889-922. Not obtained: SAGE answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge, and an archived capture of the PDF resolves to a login page. The figures here come from the abstract carried by Crossref.

Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., & Kirchner, J. Does similarity always lead to attraction? A quantitative research synthesis of the similarity effect. Undated manuscript hosted on Horton's Wabash College page under the filename of the 2008 article. Read in full; it reports 385 effect sizes from 293 investigations and is the source of the laboratory, field and publication-bias figures on this page.

Rand, T. M., & Wexley, K. N. (1975). Demonstration of the effect, 'similar to me,' in simulated employment interviews. Psychological Reports, 36(2), 535-544. Not obtained: SAGE answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge. Described from its abstract at Crossref, which states the extreme-groups selection of the 160 raters.

Sacco, J. M., Scheu, C. R., Ryan, A. M., & Schmitt, N. (2003). An investigation of race and sex similarity effects in interviews: A multilevel approach to relational demography. Journal of Applied Psychology, 88(5), 852-865. Not obtained: PsycNet, ResearchGate and CORE all refused on 21 September 2026. Described from its abstract at PubMed.

McCarthy, J. M., Van Iddekinge, C. H., & Campion, M. A. (2010). Are highly structured job interviews resistant to demographic similarity effects? Personnel Psychology, 63(2), 325-359. Full text read from the hosted copy at Rotman; the sample and the effect sizes above come from its method and results sections.

Giuliano, L., Levine, D. I., & Leonard, J. (2009). Manager race and the race of new hires. Journal of Labor Economics, 27(4), 589-631. Read as the September 2006 working paper hosted at Berkeley, whose abstract matches the published one. The published article at Chicago is behind a Cloudflare challenge.

Rivera, L. A. (2012). Hiring as cultural matching: The case of elite professional service firms. American Sociological Review, 77(6), 999-1022. Full text read from the copy hosted by the American Sociological Association.

Bertrand, M., & Mullainathan, S. (2004). Are Emily and Greg more employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A field experiment on labor market discrimination. American Economic Review, 94(4), 991-1013. Full text read from a copy hosted at the University of Chicago.

Quillian, L., Pager, D., Hexel, O., & Midtboen, A. H. (2017). Meta-analysis of field experiments shows no change in racial discrimination in hiring over time. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 114(41), 10870-10875. The publisher's site and PubMed Central both answer with a bot challenge; read in full from an Internet Archive capture of the PNAS PDF, which carries the sample counts and the confidence intervals used above.

Pompian, M. M. (2012). Affinity bias. In Behavioral Finance and Wealth Management, 253-260. The earliest indexed scholarly use of the exact phrase found in these searches. Not read: Wiley answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge.

Buzanowska, M., & Rensel, M. (2023). Get your diverse team to outperform: Navigating through affinity bias. Management in Healthcare: A Peer-Reviewed Journal, 8(1), 16. Cited as an example of where the term lives; not read.
Westover, J. (2024). Affinity Bias: An Overlook Threat to Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Efforts. Human Capital Leadership Review, 15(2). Cited as an example of where the term lives; not read.
